# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 917 ancient and classical settlements, oasis metropolises, fortified citadels (*kala* and *tepe*), caravanserai towns and pastoral mortuary centres active across Central Asia between 1000BC and 500AD (encompassing 3.890.946 km² across nine territorial basins). Synthesising regional archaeological excavation registers, the Central Asian Archaeological Landscapes (CAAL) database, Al-Thurayya historical toponymy compendium, Pleiades Classical gazetteer, and national cultural heritage registries [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Morris2021Economic; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Grenet2025Histoire; @Anon2026Reflecting], the register encompasses every primary excavated habitation node of the domain. These entries span the sprawling mudbrick capitals and Silk Road emporiums of the Kushan, Parthian, Sogdian and Khwarazmian realms led by Merv (60.000 peak residents in 500AD), Samarkand (45.000), Old Termez (38.000), Bukhara (35.000), Old Nisa (24.000), Tashkent (22.000), Kunya-Urgench (22.000), Khujand (22.000), Akhsikent (22.000), Kanka (22.000), Erkurgan (18.000), Shahrisabz (15.000) and Dalverzin-Tepe (15.000). Across the 917 catalogued entries, the gazetteer documents longitudinal occupation sequences spanning the Saka pastoral horizon, Achaemenid imperial consolidation, Hellenistic Greco-Bactrian foundations, the Kushan urban zenith and early mediaeval Hephthalite transitions. Alongside the 917 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 1.291 excluded duplicate aliases, close-pair excavation trenches and minor satellite find-spots out of 2.208 total evaluated candidate entities.

# Background

Settlement systems across Central Asia during the first millennium BC and the early first millennium AD evolved through continuous structural interaction between sedentary oasis farmers and mobile pastoralists [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Morris2021Economic; @Librado2024Widespread]. In the arid riverine lowlands of the Zeravshan, Murghab, Surkhandarya, Amu Darya and Syr Darya deltas, urbanism was sustained by massive gravity-fed irrigation networks that supported dense mudbrick towns protected by multi-tiered ramparts, deep ditches and fortified keeps (*ark* or *diz*) [@MirMakhamad2024Agricultur; @Dhawi2024Oasis; @BETTS2016Akchakhan].

During the Achaemenid and Hellenistic periods (c. 530BC to 130BC), imperial administration fostered the expansion of regional metropolises such as Marakanda (Samarkand), Antiochia Margiana (Merv), Demetrias (Old Termez) and Alexandria Eschate (Khujand), which combined indigenous Central Asian hydraulic planning with Mediterranean civic features, including orthogonal street grids, public agoras, mints and administrative archives [@Sanahuja2020Historiogr; @Francfort2020Quelques; @Morris2021Economicb]. 

Under the Kushan Empire, Arsacid Parthian Margiana, Classical Khwarazm and the Kangju confederation (c. 130BC to 350AD), urban growth attained historic dimensions [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Zhang2023Characteri]. Cities expanded beyond their fortified citadels into sprawling intramural residential sectors (*shahristan*) and extensive suburban artisanal quarters (*rabad*) containing monumental ceramic kilns, glassworks, iron smelters and Buddhist monasteries [@Morris2021Economic; @Anon2022Some]. Concurrently, along the northern and western steppes, mobile Saka, Wusun and Massagetae confederations established seasonal pastoral base camps, hilltop stone refuges and monumental kurgan necropolises (such as Issyk, Tasmola and Jety-Asar) that controlled strategic river crossings and grazing corridors [@Zairova2026Phenomenon; @Anon2026; @Cinar2026Kazakh].

# Methodology

Settlement records were assembled by systematically querying national excavation inventories, heritage registries, and published archaeological gazetteers across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Anon2026Reflecting; @Sanahuja2020Historiogr]. All 917 catalogued entries carry verified geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the nine territorial basins.

In the regional source ledger, 1.291 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair excavation trenches situated within 5 km of primary site cores, or isolated kurgan clusters and artifact scatters lacking domestic architectural remains [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Namen2025Human]. For instance, multiple excavation sectors, satellite bastions and chronologically segregated trench designations associated with Merv (Erk Kala, Gyaur Kala, Sultan Kala), Samarkand (Afrasiab sectors), Old Nisa and Toprak-Kala were consolidated into unified site entries with documented longitudinal demographic trajectories [@Morris2021Economic; @BETTS2016Akchakhan].

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 917 included settlements and 1.291 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 2.208 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 917 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates, sub-regional assignments and chronologically bounded population estimates. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading classical oasis settlements across Central Asia.

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-scythian} summarises the distribution of catalogued settlements across all nine territories alongside their leading centres. Sogdiana Core leads all regions with 196 catalogued sites, followed by Northern Bactria (158), Dayuan Ferghana and Kangju Chach (154), Classical Khwarazm (138) and Parthia-Margiana (112). Table \ref{tab:excluded-scythian} details the leading 30 of 1.291 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

## Archaeological Caveats and Taphonomic Preservation

Two primary spatial and environmental factors condition settlement analysis across Central Asia. First, modern agricultural intensification and urban expansion have disproportionately impacted ancient oasis sites [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @Dhawi2024Oasis]. Major contemporary cities such as Tashkent, Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv, Khujand and Osh sit directly atop or immediately adjacent to their classical predecessors, resulting in severe destruction of early peripheral settlement layers beneath modern infrastructure [@Anon2022Some; @MirMakhamad2024Agricultur]. In rural irrigated zones, twentieth-century Soviet land reclamation and intensive cotton monoculture levelled hundreds of smaller mudbrick tells (*tepe*), biasing gazetteer counts toward well-preserved monumental citadels in desert margins (such as Khwarazm) [@BETTS2016Akchakhan; @Dhawi2024Oasis].

Second, taphonomic visibility diverges sharply between sedentary mudbrick structures and mobile pastoralist remains [@Librado2024Widespread; @Zairova2026Phenomenon]. Mudbrick architecture in arid environments leaves prominent topographic mounds readily identifiable through satellite imagery and aerial photography [@Franklin2023Archaeolog; @BETTS2016Akchakhan]. In contrast, seasonal yurt encampments and open-air pastoral campsites along the northern steppe lack substantial architectural footprints, leaving mortuary kurgans as their primary tangible archaeological manifestation [@Zairova2026Phenomenon; @Namen2025Human]. Consequently, gazetteer densities in the northern steppes reflect burial monuments rather than domestic residential enclosures, requiring careful ethnographic calibration of pastoral group size [@Librado2024Widespread; @Armaroli2026Tracing].
